Using Generative AI in Instruction
The book does not treat generative AI as either prohibited assistance or unquestioned authority.
A useful instructional rule is:
\[
\boxed{\text{AI Assistance Does Not Transfer Analytical Responsibility}}
\]
When students use generative AI, instructors can require them to document what the tool contributed, test generated code, verify citations and APIs, inspect assumptions, identify possible leakage, and explain why the final analytical decisions are defensible.
AI Pair Programmer activities are therefore best assessed on verification and reasoning, not on whether AI was used.

Designing Assessments
Strong assessments ask students to justify decisions rather than merely produce outputs.
Instead of:

Fit three classifiers and report accuracy.

consider:

Formulate the prediction problem, justify the evaluation metric, establish a baseline, compare appropriate models using a leakage-safe workflow, analyze important errors, and explain what evidence would be required before the model should influence a real decision.

The second task assesses machine-learning judgment.

A Suggested Evaluation Lens
Across assignments and projects, instructors can evaluate five dimensions:







Dimension
Central Question




Conceptual reasoning
Does the student understand what the method is doing?


Computational implementation
Is the analysis correct, transparent, and reproducible?


Evaluation quality
Does the evidence support the performance claim?


Interpretation and responsibility
Are limitations, consequences, and domain assumptions considered?


Communication
Can another reader understand and inspect the analytical argument?



This lens works across algorithmic, applied, and research-oriented assignments.

title: Teaching with This Book
text:
Closing Perspective
A course built around this book should leave students with more than a collection of models.
They should be able to ask:

What problem is actually being solved?
What assumptions connect the data to the claim?
What evidence supports model performance?
How might the model fail?
Who could be affected?
What would make the analysis reproducible?
What would turn this application into a meaningful research contribution?

The enduring competency is not knowing which Python function to call.
It is knowing what should be done, why it is defensible, what the evidence permits us to conclude, and how another person can verify the work.

title: About the Author
text:
Teaching and Mentorship
Dr. Itauma Itauma is an Associate Professor of Data Science and Analytics at Harrisburg University of Science and Technology. His work brings together data science, artificial intelligence, machine learning, analytics, research methodology, and graduate education.
His scholarly interests include artificial intelligence and machine learning in education, health, and business; learning analytics; structural equation modeling; meta-analysis; reproducible analytics; and the use of computational methods to strengthen evidence-based decision-making.
Dr. Itauma holds a Ph.D. in Instructional Design and Technology with a concentration in Analytics, an M.S. in Computer Science, an M.S. in Computer Engineering, and an MBA. He also completed the Harvard Business Analytics Program (HBAP). His academic work has included teaching, program leadership, curriculum development, dissertation mentorship, and the development of graduate learning experiences in analytics, data science, artificial intelligence, and research.
A recurring theme in his teaching and scholarship is that technical competence is necessary but insufficient. Data scientists must also learn to question assumptions, evaluate evidence, communicate uncertainty, consider the consequences of analytical decisions, and create work that others can inspect and reproduce.
That perspective informs the philosophy of Machine Learning Using Python:
\[
\boxed{\text{Algorithms}+\text{Data}+\text{Evidence}+\text{Judgment}}
\]
The Second Edition reflects his commitment to helping students move beyond executing machine-learning libraries toward becoming thoughtful practitioners and researchers who can explain what they did, why they did it, what the evidence supports, and what remains uncertain.
Dr. Itauma’s approach to graduate education emphasizes analytical reasoning, research literacy, reproducible workflows, responsible use of artificial intelligence, and the connection between computational methods and meaningful questions.
He works with master’s and doctoral students across applied analytics and research settings, with particular interest in helping learners progress from:
\[
\text{Learning Methods}
\rightarrow
\text{Applying Methods}
\rightarrow
\text{Evaluating Evidence}
\rightarrow
\text{Producing Knowledge}.
\]

Corrections and Updates
Corrections made after this archival release should be documented through subsequent repository history and, when appropriate, a new versioned release.
A corrected release should preserve the scholarly record rather than silently replacing the state associated with an earlier archived version.
